title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
description: Published in 1845 in Boston and the founding text of the African-American literary tradition: the account of Douglass's life from his birth in slavery to his escape and his first years of freedom. It is a prose work of 1845 by Frederick Douglass; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Douglass records his separation from his mother, his learning to read, the cruelty of the slave-breaker Edward Covey and his fight with him, his escape, the means of which he deliberately withholds, and his arrival in New Bedford, and ends with his first speech at Nantucket.
narrative_structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Frederick Douglass, the narrator; Harriet Bailey, his mother; Captain Anthony; Edward Covey; Hugh and Sophia Auld; Thomas Auld; Aunt Hester; Mr Gore, the overseer
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of escape and self-making.
historical_context: The 1818-45, the slave economy of Maryland, the abolitionist movement, and the American debate on the reliability of slave testimony. The record dates the work as composed between 1844 and 1845 and first published in 1845 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum; Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: The Narrative is the central American slave narrative and the founding text of African-American literature: its account of literacy, resistance and escape set the pattern for the genre, and its eloquence made Douglass the most important black voice in the English-speaking world.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1845, as autobiography (slave narrative), by Frederick Douglass. Composed between 1844 and 1845. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?'
description: Delivered at Rochester on 5 July 1852 and published the same year: the greatest American political speech of the nineteenth century, and the most complete indictment of American hypocrisy. It is a prose work of 1852 by Frederick Douglass; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Lecture and Popular Address; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Douglass tells his audience that the Fourth of July is not his, that the slave's wrongs are shared by every American, and that the republic's professions of liberty are mocked by the slave market in the capital; he ends with a call to abolish slavery and to make the Declaration true.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of escape and self-making.
historical_context: The 1852, the Fugitive Slave Law, the abolitionist movement, and the American celebration of the Fourth of July. The record dates the work as composed in 1852 and first published in 1852 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: The Fourth of July address is the central American oration and the founding text of the black critique of American democracy: its phrases have entered the language, and it remains the most powerful statement of the gap between American ideals and American practice.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1852, as oration (corinthian hall, rochester), by Frederick Douglass. Composed in 1852. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: My Bondage and My Freedom
description: Published in 1855 and the second and fullest of Douglass's autobiographies: an expanded account of slavery and freedom that includes his break with Garrison and his own analysis of the slave system. It is a prose work of 1855 by Frederick Douglass; it belongs to Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Douglass adds to the 1845 narrative the account of his childhood, the death of his mother, the economics of the plantation, his escape, his early years as an abolitionist, his travels in Britain and Ireland, and the purchase of his freedom by British friends.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
principal_characters: Frederick Douglass, the narrator; Betsey Bailey, his grandmother; Harriet Bailey, his mother; Captain Anthony; Edward Covey; Hugh and Sophia Auld; Thomas Auld; William Lloyd Garrison
literary_form: Autobiography; review essay, first issued in 1855
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of escape and self-making.
historical_context: The 1855, the split in the abolitionist movement between Garrison and the political abolitionists, and the American debate on the Constitution and slavery. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1855 and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: My Bondage and My Freedom is the greatest of the slave narratives and the most analytically powerful: its account of slavery as an economic system and its argument for political abolition made it the central text of black political thought before the Civil War.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1855, as autobiography, by Frederick Douglass. Composed between 1854 and 1855. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Heroic Slave
description: Published in 1853 and the only work of fiction Douglass wrote: a novella based on the revolt led by Madison Washington aboard the slave ship Creole in 1841. It is a prose fiction work of 1853 by Frederick Douglass; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Imperial Adventure Romance and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Madison Washington, an enslaved Virginian who has escaped to Canada, returns to rescue his wife and is shipped to New Orleans; he leads the seizure of the Creole and sails the ship to Nassau, where the British free the rebels.
narrative_structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
principal_characters: Madison Washington; Mr Listwell, the Ohio abolitionist; Susan, his wife; Tom Grant, the Creole's first mate
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of escape and self-making.
historical_context: The 1841, the Creole case, the British abolition of slavery in the colonies, and the American debate on the legal status of slave revolt. The record dates the work as composed in 1852 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance, it is catalogued under sensation novel; imperial adventure romance.
literary_significance: The Heroic Slave is the first American work of fiction by a black writer and the founding text of African-American fiction: it invented the black revolutionary hero of American literature and made the slave revolt a subject of the American imagination.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1853, as novella (in autographs for freedom, 1853), by Frederick Douglass. Composed in 1852. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
description: Published in 1881 and revised in 1892: the last and longest of Douglass's autobiographies, covering the Civil War, emancipation and the disappointments of Reconstruction. It is a prose work of 1881 by Frederick Douglass; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Douglass recounts his escape, his abolitionist career, his recruitment of black troops in the Civil War, his meetings with Lincoln, his service as marshal of the District of Columbia and minister to Haiti, and his growing despair at the betrayal of the freedpeople.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
principal_characters: Frederick Douglass, the narrator; Abraham Lincoln; John Brown; William Lloyd Garrison; Anna Murray Douglass; Thomas Auld
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of escape and self-making.
historical_context: The 1881-92, the Civil War and Reconstruction, the withdrawal of federal troops in 1877, the rise of Jim Crow, and the American debate on the Negro problem. The record dates the work as composed between 1880 and 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Life and Times is the central American autobiography of the nineteenth century and the fullest record of the black experience from slavery to the nadir of race relations: it is the essential document of Reconstruction and of the failure of American emancipation.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1881, as autobiography (revised and expanded 1892), by Frederick Douglass. Composed between 1880 and 1881. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself
description: Published in 1861 under the pseudonym Linda Brent and the first full-length slave narrative by a woman: the account of Harriet Jacobs's life in slavery and of her seven years hiding in a garret. It is a prose work of 1861 by Harriet Jacobs; it belongs to Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Linda Brent is pursued by her master Dr Flint, becomes the mother of two children by a white lawyer, hides for seven years in a tiny garret above her grandmother's shed, escapes to the North, and after the Fugitive Slave Law is forced to hide again; she is finally freed and works as a nurse.
narrative_structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Linda Brent (Harriet Jacobs), the narrator; Dr Flint; Mrs Flint; Mr Sands; Aunt Martha, her grandmother; Benny and Ellen, her children; William, her brother; Mrs Bruce
literary_form: Autobiography (slave narrative; published as Linda Brent, edited by Lydia Maria Child)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is first-person retrospective narrative with direct appeal to the reader.
historical_context: The 1820s-50s, the slave society of Edenton, North Carolina, the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850, and the abolitionist movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1858 and 1860 and first published in 1861 and the corpus places it within Dark Romance and the Puritan Inheritance; Transcendentalism and the Concord Lyceum, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: Incidents is a founding text of African-American women's writing and of American autobiography: it is the first slave narrative to make the sexual exploitation of enslaved women its central subject, and its seven-year hiding is one of the most extraordinary acts of resistance in American history.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Linda Brent. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1861, by Harriet Jacobs. Composed between 1858 and 1860. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Letters and Relief Work among the Freedpeople
description: Written between 1862 and 1868 while Jacobs worked among the freedpeople of Alexandria and Savannah, and published in the American Freedman and the abolitionist press. It is a prose work of 1862 by Harriet Jacobs; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Review Essay and Quarterly Argument.
plot_or_argument: Jacobs describes the condition of the refugees, the schools, the hospitals, the treatment of the women and children, and the obstacles placed in the way of the freedpeople by the army and by the government.
narrative_structure: A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Harriet Jacobs, the writer; Louisa Jacobs, her daughter; the freedpeople of Alexandria and Savannah

Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The text is the dated entry, continuous in its observation. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is first-person retrospective narrative with direct appeal to the reader.
historical_context: The 1862-68, the Civil War and Reconstruction, the contraband camps, and the Freedmen's Bureau. The record dates the work as composed between 1862 and 1868 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: Jacobs's relief work and reports are a significant primary document of Reconstruction and of the freedpeople's experience, and they extend her literary achievement into the history of American social reform.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1862, as letters, reports and journalism, by Harriet Jacobs. Composed between 1862 and 1868. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Lady Audley's Secret
description: Serialised in 1861-62 and published in three volumes: the most successful of all English sensation novels, and the one that made the beauties of the genre into a serious argument about the law. It is a prose fiction work of 1862 by Mary Elizabeth Braddon; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Detective Story and the Tale of Detection and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Robert Audley investigates the disappearance of his friend George Talboys and comes to suspect that his uncle's beautiful young wife, Lady Audley, is George's supposedly dead wife Helen; he pursues her through a series of disguises to a private asylum in Belgium, and the novel ends with her confession and her retirement to a maison de sante, and with Robert's marriage to Clara Talboys.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Lady Audley (Helen Talboys); Robert Audley; George Talboys; Sir Michael Audley; Alicia Audley; Clara Talboys; Luke Marks; Phoebe Marks; Dr Mosgrave
literary_form: Sensation novel (serialised in Robin Goodfellow and the Sixpenny Magazine, 1861-62; three volumes 1862)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is rapid, incident-packed serial plotting.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, the private lunatic asylum trade, and the circulating-library market for three-volume fiction. The record dates the work as composed between 1861 and 1862 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; detective story and the tale of detection.
literary_significance: Lady Audley's Secret is the central English sensation novel and one of the most important Victorian novels about the legal and social position of women: its heroine's crime is the logical response to a world in which a poor woman has no legal existence of her own, and the novel's use of the asylum to silence her is a direct indictment of Victorian psychiatry.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as M. E. Braddon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in Temple Bar and in Robin Goodfellow from October 1861 and published in three volumes by Tinsley Brothers in October 1862. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Aurora Floyd
description: Published in 1863 and Braddon's second great sensation novel: the story of an heiress with a violent temper, a secret marriage and a husband who may return at any moment. It is a prose fiction work of 1863 by Mary Elizabeth Braddon; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Aurora Floyd, the daughter of a banker, secretly marries the groom James Conyers and pays him to disappear; she later marries the landowner John Mellish, and Conyers's return leads to his murder, the trial of Mellish, and the eventual discovery that the killer is Aurora's cousin's husband.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Aurora Floyd; John Mellish; Talbot Bulstrode; James Conyers; Lucy Floyd; Archibald Floyd; Matthew Harrison; Eliza
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is rapid, incident-packed serial plotting.
historical_context: The 1860s, the horse-racing and betting world, the railway, and the marriage law. The record dates the work as composed between 1862 and 1863 and first published in 1863 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; new woman and marriage-question novel.
literary_significance: Aurora Floyd is the fullest sensation treatment of the woman with a secret past and one of the earliest English novels to give a heroine an aggressive, physical energy — riding, hunting, fighting — that the period associated with men.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as M. E. Braddon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Tinsley Brothers in January 1863, after serialisation in Temple Bar in 1862. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Doctor's Wife
description: Published in 1864 and a deliberate English answer to Flaubert's Madame Bovary: the story of a doctor's wife whose reading of novels fills her with romantic expectations her marriage cannot satisfy. It is a prose fiction work of 1864 by Mary Elizabeth Braddon; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel; Realist Novel of Common Life and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Isabel Sleaford marries the good, dull country doctor George Gilbert, drifts into a romantic friendship with the wealthy poet-squire Roland Lansdell and refuses to elope with him; her husband dies of fever, Lansdell is fatally beaten by her father, a returned convict, and Isabel, widowed and left Lansdell's fortune, devotes it to good works.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
principal_characters: Isabel Sleaford (Isabel Gilbert); George Gilbert; Roland Lansdell; Jacob Sleaford, Isabel's father; Sigismund Smith; Charles Raymond
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is rapid, incident-packed serial plotting.
historical_context: The 1860s, the circulating-library novel and its female readers, the medical profession, and the English reception of French realism. The record dates the work as composed in 1864 and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: The Doctor's Wife is the most self-conscious English novel about the novel-reading woman: it takes the French realist diagnosis of romantic reading and turns it into a defence of English domestic life, and it is a key text for the history of the woman reader.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as M. E. Braddon. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1864, as novel (three volumes), by Mary Elizabeth Braddon. Composed in 1864. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Uncle Silas: A Tale of Bartram-Haugh
description: Published in 1864 and the finest of Le Fanu's novels: the story of a young heiress left in the power of her sinister uncle in a remote Derbyshire house. It is a prose fiction work of 1864 by Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Maud Ruthyn, whose father has made her uncle Silas her guardian, goes to Bartram-Haugh, where Silas — a ruined gambler suspected of the murder of a moneylender — and his governess Madame de la Rougierre conspire to marry her to Silas's son Dudley and, when that fails, to murder her; she escapes with the help of her cousin Monica and the servant Mary Quince.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Maud Ruthyn; Silas Ruthyn; Austin Ruthyn; Madame de la Rougierre; Dudley Ruthyn; Monica Knollys; Mary Quince; Godfrey Knollys; Dr Bryerly; Tom Brice
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the 'case' narrative framed by a medical or antiquarian editor.
historical_context: The 1860s, the power of a guardian under English law, the private asylum and the fortune-hunting of the impoverished gentry. The record dates the work as composed in 1864 and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1864, as novel (three volumes), by Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu. Composed in 1864. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Carmilla
description: Published in the collection In a Glass Darkly in 1872 and the founding text of the lesbian vampire narrative: the story of a young woman in Styria who is visited by a beautiful guest who is not alive.
plot_or_argument: Laura, the daughter of a retired Austrian officer, is visited as a child and then as a young woman by Carmilla, who is in fact the revenant of the Countess Mircalla Karnstein; Laura weakens, a peasant girl dies, and Baron Vordenburg traces the vampire to the ruined chapel of Karnstein, where she is destroyed.
narrative_structure: A first-person memoir framed by the case notes of Dr Martin Hesselius. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Laura; Carmilla (Mircalla, Countess Karnstein); General Spielsdorf; Baron Vordenburg; Laura's father; Bertha Rheinfeldt; Madame Perrodon
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is the 'case' narrative framed by a medical or antiquarian editor.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Austrian frontier and its folklore, the Gothic tradition of the vampire from Polidori, and the Victorian medical discourse on hysteria. The record dates the work as composed between 1871 and 1872 and first published in 1872 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; sensation novel.
literary_significance: Carmilla is the most influential vampire story before Dracula and the origin of the female vampire in English literature; its treatment of an intense attachment between two women has made it the founding text of the queer Gothic.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as J. Sheridan Le Fanu. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1872, as novella (in in a glass darkly, 1872), by Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu. Composed between 1871 and 1872. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The House by the Churchyard

title: The Cloister and the Hearth: A Tale of the Middle Ages
alternative_titles: Cloister and the Hearth: A Tale of the Middle Ages
description: Published in 1861 and the greatest English historical novel of the Middle Ages: the story of Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou, who travels from Holland to Rome in the fifteenth century in search of the woman he loves, and becomes the father of Erasmus.
plot_or_argument: Gerard, an illuminator's son, loves Margaret Brandt but is driven from home by his father; he travels through Burgundy, France and Italy, is imprisoned, joins a company of soldiers and survives a series of picaresque adventures, while Margaret bears his son and dies before his return; Gerard becomes a priest and the novel ends with the boy Erasmus at the age of reason.

The author's characteristic manner is the dossier method: documents, letters, newspaper extracts and trial evidence worked into narrative.

The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1861 and first published in 1861 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; realist novel of common life.

title: Hard Cash: A Matter-of-Fact Romance

title: It Is Never Too Late to Mend: A Matter-of-Fact Romance
alternative_titles: It Is Never Too Late to Mend
description: Published in 1856 and Reade's first documentary novel: a triple narrative of the English prison system, the Australian goldfields and a rural rivalry in love, designed to expose the cruelty of the separate system.
plot_or_argument: George Fielding, a struggling Berkshire farmer, goes to the Australian goldfields to make the fortune that will let him marry Susan Merton, while the thief Tom Robinson passes through the brutal regime of a county gaol under the governor Hawes until the chaplain Eden reforms it; the prison chapters record, with documentary fidelity, the treadmill, the crank and the separate system. Transported to Australia, Robinson becomes George's partner on the diggings, and the two return to defeat the scheming Meadows, George's rival for Susan.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.

title: Cometh Up as a Flower
description: Published in 1867 and Broughton's sensational first novel: a first-person narrative of a woman who loves one man, marries another for money, and dies of the consequences. title: Red as a Rose Is She
description: Published in 1870 and the best of Broughton's early novels: the story of a high-spirited girl of small means whose passionate, quarrelsome love for a richer man survives pride, separation and a near-fatal illness.
plot_or_argument: Esther Craye, a high-spirited girl of small means, meets St John Gerard on a country-house visit and falls passionately in love, though he is expected to marry the cold beauty Constance Blessington; quarrels, pride and Esther's poverty part them, she goes out to earn her own living, and only a near-fatal illness brings the lovers to marriage.

title: Belinda. A Novel
description: Published in 1883 and the novel that made Broughton a satirist: the story of a young woman whose reticence loses her the man she loves and who marries in despair an elderly pedant, Broughton's portrait of Mark Pattison.
plot_or_argument: In Dresden Belinda Churchill falls in love with the young David Rivers, but her shyness reads as coldness and their understanding is left unspoken; when he is called home and never writes, she marries in despair the elderly, humourless Professor Forth, her sister Sarah's discarded fiancé, and three days after the wedding receives the letter that shows her mistake. The rest of the novel tests her loyalty to a loveless marriage.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.

title: Under Two Flags
description: Published in 1867 and the most popular of Ouida's novels: the story of a guardsman who takes the blame for a forgery, enlists under a false name in the French army in Algeria, and wins glory there. title: Moths
description: Published in 1880 and the most notorious of Ouida's society novels: the story of a beautiful, bored aristocrat married to a man she does not love, and of the cosmopolitan world that destroys her. It is a prose fiction work of 1880 by Ouida; it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
plot_or_argument: Vere Herbert, an innocent girl of seventeen, is married off by her worldly mother, Lady Dolly, to the brutal Russian Prince Zouroff; she loves the great tenor Corrèze but stays faithful through years of a degrading marriage among the 'moths' of fashionable society in London and Paris, until Zouroff divorces her and she goes to Corrèze, whose voice has been destroyed.

title: A Dog of Flanders
description: Published in 1872 and one of the most beloved animal stories in the world: the tale of Nello, a poor Flemish boy, and his dog Patrasche, who dream of seeing Rubens's triptych in Antwerp cathedral. title: New Grub Street
description: Published in 1891 and the central English novel about the literary profession: the parallel stories of a scholar who cannot sell his work and a journalist who can sell anything. Biffen's realistic slum novel, Mr Bailey, Grocer, is published to no effect.

title: The Odd Women
description: Published in 1893 and the most important English novel of the 'surplus women' question: the story of three sisters, the plain women who must support themselves, and of two sisters' very different answers to their situation.

title: The Nether World
